intro: Seated in a ship by the sea while great multitudes stood on the shore, Jesus "spake many things unto them in parables" (Matthew 13:1-3). This is one of the parables He told that day about the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 13:24).

questions.prompt: According to the parable, when did the enemy come and sow tares among the wheat?
options: While men slept
At the time of harvest
At noon, while the servants watched the field
After the wheat had been gathered into the barn
questions.explanation: Matthew 13:25 says that "while men slept, his enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat, and went his way."
questions.hint: The enemy did his work at a time when no one was watching.

questions.prompt: Why did the householder tell his servants not to gather up the tares right away?
options: Lest they root up also the wheat with them
Because the tares would wither on their own
Because the tares were good to eat
Because the field belonged to the enemy
questions.explanation: In Matthew 13:29 he answered, "Nay; lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them."
questions.hint: His concern was for the good crop growing alongside the bad.

questions.prompt: In Jesus' own explanation of the parable, what does the harvest represent?
options: The end of the world
The preaching of John the Baptist
The feast of the Passover
The rebuilding of the temple
keywords: the harvest is the end of the world
questions.explanation: Jesus states in Matthew 13:39 that "the harvest is the end of the world; and the reapers are the angels."
questions.hint: Look at how Jesus identifies the harvest and the reapers together in His explanation.

questions.prompt: Who asked Jesus to explain this parable, and where were they?
options: His disciples, in the house after He sent the multitude away
The Pharisees, in the synagogue
The multitude, on the shore of the sea
The servants of the high priest, in the temple
questions.explanation: Matthew 13:36 records that Jesus "sent the multitude away, and went into the house: and his disciples came unto him, saying, Declare unto us the parable of the tares of the field."
questions.hint: The explanation was given privately, after the crowd had gone.

intro: In the temple at Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the people challenged Jesus, asking, 'By what authority doest thou these things?' (Matthew 21:23). After answering them with a question and the parable of the two sons, Jesus continued, 'Hear another parable' (Matthew 21:33).

questions.prompt: When the householder sent his servants to receive the fruits of the vineyard, how did the husbandmen treat them?
options: They beat one, killed another, and stoned another
They paid them half the fruits and sent them away
They welcomed them and gave them all the fruits
They bound them and sent them to the king
questions.explanation: The husbandmen 'took his servants, and beat one, and killed another, and stoned another,' and they treated the next, larger group of servants 'likewise' (Matthew 21:35-36).
questions.hint: The servants received violence, not fruit.

questions.prompt: When the husbandmen saw the householder's son coming, what did they say among themselves?
options: Let us give him the fruits, for he is the lord's son
This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance
Let us flee into a far country before he comes
Let us send him back to his father with a gift
questions.explanation: Though the father said 'They will reverence my son,' the husbandmen said, 'This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance,' and they cast him out and slew him (Matthew 21:37-39).
questions.hint: They wanted what would one day belong to the son.

questions.prompt: After quoting the scripture about the stone which the builders rejected, what did Jesus say would happen to the kingdom of God?
options: It would be given to the chief priests as a reward
It would be delayed until the husbandmen repented
It would be taken from them and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof
It would be divided equally among all the husbandmen
questions.explanation: Jesus said, 'The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof' (Matthew 21:43).
questions.hint: Think of what the householder wanted from his vineyard all along.

questions.prompt: When the chief priests and Pharisees perceived that Jesus spoke of them, why did they not lay hands on him at that time?
options: Because the Roman governor forbade it
Because they agreed with the parable and repented
Because it was the sabbath day
Because they feared the multitude, who took him for a prophet
questions.explanation: Though they sought to lay hands on him, 'they feared the multitude, because they took him for a prophet' (Matthew 21:46).
questions.hint: Consider how the crowds around Jesus regarded him.

intro: While Jesus was teaching in the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people challenged him: 'By what authority doest thou these things?' (Matthew 21:23). After they declined to answer his counter-question, saying 'We cannot tell' (Matthew 21:27), he asked them, 'But what think ye?' and told them a story (Matthew 21:28).

questions.prompt: What did the father ask his first son to do?
options: Go work to day in his vineyard
Feed the swine in the field
Gather the harvest into his barn
Go up to Jerusalem to pay tribute
questions.explanation: The father came to the first son and said, 'Son, go work to day in my vineyard' (Matthew 21:28).
questions.hint: Think of a place where grapes are grown.

questions.prompt: How did the second son respond when the father gave him the same request?
options: He said, 'I go, sir,' and went not
He said, 'I will not,' but afterward repented and went
He went without saying a word
He asked to take his brother's place
questions.explanation: The second son answered, 'I go, sir: and went not' (Matthew 21:30), the opposite of the first son, who refused but later repented and went (Matthew 21:29).
questions.hint: Compare his words with his actions.

questions.prompt: After his hearers answered that the first son did his father's will, what did Jesus tell them?
options: That the publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before them
That both sons would receive an equal inheritance
That the second son would be cast into outer darkness
That they had answered wrongly
questions.explanation: When they said 'The first,' Jesus replied, 'Verily I say unto you, That the publicans and the harlots go into the kingdom of God before you' (Matthew 21:31).
questions.hint: Jesus names two groups that his religious listeners looked down on.

questions.prompt: In explaining his point, Jesus connected the parable to John. What did he say about how his hearers responded to John?
options: They believed him not, and when they saw others believe, they repented not afterward
They believed him at first but later turned away
They believed him, but the publicans and harlots did not
They never heard John's preaching at all
questions.explanation: Jesus said John came 'in the way of righteousness, and ye believed him not: but the publicans and the harlots believed him,' and even after seeing it they 'repented not afterward' (Matthew 21:32). This ties back to the earlier question about John's baptism (Matthew 21:25).
questions.hint: Recall the counter-question Jesus asked earlier about John's baptism, and who in verse 32 did believe.

intro: Some who were present told Jesus of the Galilaeans 'whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices' (Luke 13:1). Jesus answered them, and then 'spake also this parable' about a fig tree in a vineyard (Luke 13:6).

questions.prompt: For how long had the owner of the vineyard come seeking fruit on the fig tree without finding any?
options: Three years
Seven years
One year
Twelve years
questions.explanation: The owner told the dresser, 'Behold, these three years I come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and find none' (Luke 13:7).
questions.hint: Look at the owner's complaint to the dresser of his vineyard.

questions.prompt: When the owner ordered the tree cut down, what did the dresser of the vineyard ask to do instead?
options: Let it alone this year also, and dig about it and dung it
Transplant it to a better part of the vineyard
Graft new branches onto it from another tree
Cut it down at once and plant a vine in its place
questions.explanation: The dresser answered, 'Lord, let it alone this year also, till I shall dig about it, and dung it' (Luke 13:8).
questions.hint: He asked for more time and offered to tend the tree himself.

questions.prompt: According to the dresser, what was to happen if the tree still bore no fruit after the extra year of care?
options: It would be cut down
It would be left standing forever
It would be given to another husbandman
It would be burned along with the whole vineyard
questions.explanation: The dresser said, 'if it bear fruit, well: and if not, then after that thou shalt cut it down' (Luke 13:9), so the extra year was a final opportunity, not an endless delay.
questions.hint: The dresser's request had a condition and a deadline.

questions.prompt: Just before this parable, Jesus spoke of the Galilaeans slain by Pilate and the eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell. What did he say about them and about his hearers?
options: They were not sinners above others; and except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish
They were sinners above all others, so his hearers had nothing to fear
Such disasters fall only on the wicked, so the righteous need not repent
Their deaths were a sign that the end of the world had come
questions.explanation: Jesus asked whether those victims were sinners above all others and answered, 'I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish' (Luke 13:3, 5). He then told the parable of the fig tree given one more year to bear fruit (Luke 13:6-9).
questions.hint: Jesus gave the same answer twice, once for each tragedy.

intro: After Jesus finished praying in a certain place, one of his disciples asked him, "Lord, teach us to pray" (Luke 11:1). Jesus gave them a pattern of prayer (Luke 11:2-4) and then told this story to his disciples (Luke 11:5).

questions.prompt: At midnight, what does the man ask his friend to lend him?
options: Three loaves
Two fishes
A lamp and oil
A jar of wine
questions.explanation: The man goes at midnight and says, "Friend, lend me three loaves," because a traveling friend has arrived and he has nothing to set before him (Luke 11:5-6).
questions.hint: Think of what a host would need to set before a hungry guest.

questions.prompt: What reason does the friend inside the house give for not getting up?
options: He has no food left in the house
The door is shut and his children are with him in bed
He is too sick to rise
He does not recognize the voice at the door
questions.explanation: He answers from within, "Trouble me not: the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give thee" (Luke 11:7).
questions.hint: Picture a household already settled down for the night.

questions.prompt: According to Jesus, why does the friend finally rise and give him as many as he needs?
options: Because he is his friend
Because he is paid for the bread
Because of the man's importunity
Because the children wake up hungry
questions.explanation: Jesus says that though he will not rise because he is his friend, "yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needeth" (Luke 11:8).
questions.hint: Jesus explicitly rules out friendship as the reason; consider the asker's persistence.

questions.prompt: In his closing comparison with earthly fathers, what does Jesus say the heavenly Father will give to them that ask him?
options: Silver and gold
A sign from heaven
Victory over their enemies
The Holy Spirit
questions.explanation: Jesus reasons that if earthly fathers know how to give good gifts to their children, "how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?" (Luke 11:13).
questions.hint: Look at the very last verse of the passage.

intro: In the temple during His final days in Jerusalem, Jesus was answering the chief priests and Pharisees, who had perceived that His previous parables were spoken about them (Matthew 21:45-46). Matthew 22:1 says He 'spake unto them again by parables,' and this story of a king's wedding feast follows.

questions.prompt: When the king's servants announced that the dinner was ready, how did some of the bidden guests respond?
options: They made light of it and went their ways, one to his farm, another to his merchandise
They said they had bought five yoke of oxen and had married a wife
They came to the wedding but left before the dinner was served
They asked the king to postpone the marriage until after the harvest
questions.explanation: Matthew 22:5 says the bidden guests 'made light of it, and went their ways, one to his farm, another to his merchandise,' even after being told all things were ready (Matthew 22:4).
questions.hint: Think of ordinary daily business that pulled them away.

questions.prompt: When the king asked a guest how he came in without a wedding garment, how did the man respond?
options: He blamed the servants for bringing him in from the highways
He was speechless
He said he was too poor to buy one
He begged the king for forgiveness
questions.explanation: Matthew 22:12 records the king's question, 'Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment?' and states simply, 'And he was speechless.'
questions.hint: The man offered no excuse at all.

questions.prompt: With what closing statement does Jesus sum up the parable?
options: So the last shall be first, and the first last
Whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased
For many are called, but few are chosen
The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few
questions.explanation: Jesus ends the parable in Matthew 22:14 with the words, 'For many are called, but few are chosen.'
questions.hint: The saying contrasts an invitation with a selection.

questions.prompt: Immediately after this parable, what did the Pharisees do?
options: They believed on Him and were baptized
They went away and held a feast of their own
They asked Him to explain the parable privately
They took counsel how they might entangle Him in His talk
questions.explanation: Matthew 22:15 says, 'Then went the Pharisees, and took counsel how they might entangle him in his talk,' leading to their question about tribute to Caesar.
questions.hint: Read the very next verse after the parable ends; their response was hostile.

batch.title: The Marriage of the King's Son

intro: After sending the multitude away, Jesus went into the house, and his disciples came to him asking him to declare the parable of the tares (Matthew 13:36). Continuing his private teaching, he gave them three more short pictures of the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 13:44-50).

questions.prompt: In the first parable, what did the man do after he found the treasure hid in a field?
options: He hid it, then for joy sold all that he had and bought the field
He dug it up at once and carried it away by night
He reported it to the owner of the field and asked for a reward
He divided it among his neighbours
questions.explanation: Matthew 13:44 says that when the man found the treasure he hid it, and for joy went and sold all that he had and bought that field.
questions.hint: He did not take the treasure right away. Think about what he needed to own first.

questions.prompt: What did the merchant man, who was seeking goodly pearls, do when he found one pearl of great price?
options: He went and sold all that he had, and bought it
He traded it for many smaller pearls
He gave it to the king as a gift
He left it, because he could not afford it
questions.explanation: Matthew 13:46 says that when the merchant found one pearl of great price, he went and sold all that he had and bought it.
questions.hint: His response is like that of the man in the field.

questions.prompt: In explaining the parable of the net, whom does Jesus say will come forth at the end of the world to sever the wicked from among the just?
options: The angels
The fishermen of Galilee
The scribes and Pharisees
The disciples
questions.explanation: Jesus says in Matthew 13:49 that at the end of the world the angels shall come forth and sever the wicked from among the just.
questions.hint: Jesus names the ones who do the sorting. They are not human.

questions.prompt: After asking his disciples whether they had understood all these things, Jesus said that every scribe instructed unto the kingdom of heaven is like what?
options: A householder who brings forth out of his treasure things new and old
A merchant who sells all his pearls for a field
A fisherman who casts away every fish he catches
A man who hides his treasure so that no one may find it
questions.explanation: After the disciples answered 'Yea, Lord,' Jesus said in Matthew 13:52 that every instructed scribe is like a householder who brings forth out of his treasure things new and old.
questions.hint: This picture also involves treasure, but the man shares it instead of hiding it.

batch.title: The Hidden Treasure, the Pearl and the Net

intro: In Luke 17:20-37, after the Pharisees asked when the kingdom of God should come, Jesus taught his disciples about the days of the Son of man. Luke 18:1 then tells us that he spake a parable unto them, about a judge and a widow in a certain city.

questions.prompt: How does Jesus describe the judge in this parable?
options: He feared not God, neither regarded man
He was a righteous man who feared God
He was a priest who served in the temple
He was the widow's own brother
questions.explanation: Luke 18:2 says there was in a city a judge "which feared not God, neither regarded man." He had no reverence for God and no concern for people.
questions.hint: Jesus describes his attitude toward both God and people, and neither is favorable.

questions.prompt: When the judge finally decided to help the widow, what reason did he give within himself?
options: He had come to fear God
He wanted the people of the city to honor him
Her continual coming would weary him
The law of Moses commanded him to do it
questions.explanation: In Luke 18:4-5 the judge admits he fears not God nor regards man, yet says, "because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me."
questions.hint: His motive had nothing to do with God or justice; think about her persistence.

questions.prompt: After saying "Hear what the unjust judge saith," what does Jesus declare God will do for his own elect who cry day and night unto him?
options: He will make them wait until they stop asking
He will avenge them speedily
He will give them riches and long life
He will send them to another judge
questions.explanation: In Luke 18:7-8 Jesus asks, "shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him?" and answers, "I tell you that he will avenge them speedily."
questions.hint: Jesus contrasts God with the unjust judge; consider how quickly God acts.

questions.prompt: According to the narrator at the opening of the passage, to what end did Jesus speak this parable?
options: That men ought always to pray, and not to faint
That judges should fear God and regard man
That widows should not go to court
That men should sell all they have and give to the poor
questions.explanation: Luke 18:1 states plainly that Jesus spake this parable "to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint."
questions.hint: Look at the very first verse, before the story itself begins.

intro: While Jesus was eating bread on the sabbath in the house of one of the chief Pharisees (Luke 14:1), a fellow guest at the table spoke up, and Jesus answered him with this story (Luke 14:15-16).

questions.prompt: When the supper was prepared, what message did the man send his servant to give to those who had been invited?
options: Come; for all things are now ready.
The supper is delayed until the morning.
Bring a gift worthy of the master's table.
Only the first to arrive may enter.
questions.explanation: The servant was sent at supper time to tell the invited guests, "Come; for all things are now ready" (Luke 14:17).
questions.hint: The invitation stressed that nothing was left to prepare.

questions.prompt: One invited guest did not even ask to be excused but simply said, "I cannot come." What reason did he give?
options: He had bought a piece of ground and had to go see it.
He had married a wife.
He had bought five yoke of oxen to prove them.
He had to bury his father.
questions.explanation: The third guest said, "I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come" (Luke 14:20), unlike the first two who asked to be excused.
questions.hint: His excuse concerned a new household, not property or livestock.

questions.prompt: How does the master close the story, stating what will happen to the men who were first invited?
options: They will be given seats of honour when they finally arrive.
They will be invited again to a second supper.
None of them shall taste of his supper.
They must pay for the food that was prepared.
questions.explanation: After filling his house with others, the master declares, "none of those men which were bidden shall taste of my supper" (Luke 14:24).
questions.hint: Think about what the refusers lose by turning down the invitation.

questions.prompt: In the parable the master sends for the poor, the maimed, the halt, and the blind. Just before the parable, what had Jesus told his host to do with a similar list of people?
options: Give them alms at the door but not seat them.
Call them when making a feast, for they cannot recompense him.
Send them away so that friends and rich neighbours may come.
Seat them in the lowest room at the table.
questions.explanation: Jesus told the one who bade him, "when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind," adding that he would be blessed because they cannot recompense him (Luke 14:13-14).
questions.hint: Read the advice Jesus gave to the man who had invited him, just before verse 15.

intro: Jesus was eating in the house of a Pharisee named Simon when a woman of the city, known as a sinner, came and anointed His feet. Simon said within himself that a true prophet would know what manner of woman was touching Him, and Jesus answered with this short story addressed to Simon (Luke 7:36-40).

questions.prompt: In Jesus' story, how much did the two debtors owe the creditor?
options: One owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty
One owed a thousand talents, and the other a hundred
Each owed fifty pence
One owed ten pence, and the other one pence
questions.explanation: Jesus said a certain creditor had two debtors: 'the one owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty' (Luke 7:41).
questions.hint: One debt was ten times the size of the other.

questions.prompt: When neither debtor had anything to pay, what did the creditor do?
options: He cast them both into prison
He forgave only the one who owed less
He frankly forgave them both
He gave them more time and demanded interest
questions.explanation: Luke 7:42 says, 'when they had nothing to pay, he frankly forgave them both.'
questions.hint: The creditor treated both debtors the same way.

questions.prompt: Jesus asked Simon which debtor would love the creditor most. What did Simon answer, which Jesus said was rightly judged?
options: The one who had been forgiven least
Neither, since debts cannot produce love
Both would love him equally
The one to whom he forgave most
questions.explanation: Simon answered, 'I suppose that he, to whom he forgave most,' and Jesus replied, 'Thou hast rightly judged' (Luke 7:43).
questions.hint: Think about the size of each debt that was cancelled.

questions.prompt: Turning to the woman, Jesus contrasted her actions with Simon's. Which courtesy did Jesus say Simon had not given Him when He entered the house?
options: He gave no bread for the meal
He gave no water for His feet
He gave no seat at the table
He gave no wine to drink
questions.explanation: Jesus told Simon, 'thou gavest me no water for my feet: but she hath washed my feet with tears,' and likewise noted Simon gave no kiss and no oil (Luke 7:44-46).
questions.hint: The woman supplied this lack with her tears.
